question.text:
Which assertion is true for every function f infinitely differentiable on a neighborhood of zero?
(A) Its Taylor series has positive radius of convergence.
(B) Its Taylor series equals f near zero.
(C) If all derivatives at zero vanish, then f vanishes nearby.
(n)
(D) If f has a power-series representation near zero, its coefficients are uniquely f (0)/n!.
(E) Its Taylor series converges for every real x.

solution.text:
Termwise differentiation of any power-series representation forces the coefficient formula
and hence uniqueness. Smoothness alone does not imply a convergent or faithful Taylor

question.text:
A real function f is analytic on a neighborhood of zero and f (1/n) = 0 for every sufficiently
large integer n. What must be true?
(A) f is odd near zero.
(B) f is identically zero on some neighborhood of zero.
(C) f has a nonzero derivative of finite order at zero.
(D) Its Taylor series has radius zero.
(E) f is zero for every real argument.

solution.text:
Continuity first gives f (0) = 0. If its first nonzero Taylor coefficient had index m, then
m
f(x) = x (c + o(1)) with c ̸= 0, which cannot have nonzero zeros arbitrarily close to
zero. Thus every Taylor coefficient vanishes. Analyticity makes f zero near zero, but no
assumption controls values outside the given neighborhood.

Suppose f is infinitely differentiable near zero and f (0) = (n!) for every n ≥ 0. What is the
radius of convergence of its Maclaurin series?
(A) 0 (B) 1/2 (C) 1 (D) 2 (E) ∞

solution.text:
(n)
The Taylor coefficient is f (0)/n! = n!. The ratio of successive absolute terms is (n + 1)|x|,
so the Taylor series diverges for every x ̸= 0. Smoothness does not guarantee any positive
radius of convergence; this is distinct from a flat function whose Taylor series converges but
does not represent the function.

question.text:
If f is analytic near zero and all its odd derivatives at zero vanish, which holds sufficiently near
zero?
(A) f (x) = 0 (B) f(−x) = f(x)
(C) f is constant (D) f is a polynomial
(E) f(−x) = −f(x)

solution.text:
Analyticity represents f by its Taylor series. Only even powers occur, so changing x to −x
leaves the sum unchanged; smoothness alone would not suffice.
